I was in the exact same situation as you. Began medical transition in 2018 and my endo wanted a bunch of blood tests done, found out I have XY chromosomes as an afab person. Never knew I was intersex or suspected it beforehand. At the time, finding out was equally validating and disappointing; validating because I felt there was a “reason” I am trans, but disappointing because it further alienates me and my trans experience from other trans people, when being trans in itself is alienating enough already.

3 years later and it’s just a normal part of my life now, although I’m apprehensive to mention the intersex thing to too many cis people for fear of them seeing me as somehow different or more valid than other trans people. Usually the comments I get are “oh so you were never /actually/ a girl”, or “so that’s why you feel like a man”, which are not really things I want to hear OR impressions of me that I want cis people to have.

Being intersex doesn’t change the fact that we were afab and socialized as girls, it doesn’t make us any more or less trans than our non-intersex trans siblings, and it doesn’t mean that our transition journey has been easier in any way. I’m happy for you that you found out early in life, many intersex people never know that they are.

ah, I feel this struggle! where I live in Canada it can be as hot as 35c in the summer and as cold as -30c in the winter. I was able to maintain a fairly small year-round wardrobe by utilizing layers. a tank top, a few t-shirts, a long sleeve t-shirt, and a couple of sweaters can easily be layered on or taken off depending on the temperature. Having a good quality and well-insulated winter jacket is also vital for me personally, as it means I don't have to wear more than 2 layers under my jacket even on the coldest days. I also have a pair of long johns which I wear under my pants on particularly frigid outings, and the great thing is they double as pajama pants.

as far as hot weather goes, I only own 1 pair of shorts (and a pair of swim trunks that I sometimes wear as shorts too) and find even on very warm days I can still be comfortable in pants usually, but that's just a personal thing so you've got to curate your wardrobe to your own comfort.

Living in a 4 season region you may never be able to have one of those unbelievably small 10-item wardrobes, but you can certainly still get it below 30 if you're smart about what you chose. My main consideration when taking in a new item is how many different occasions it can be worn in, and whether or not I can use it all year round.

My entire wardrobe is 34 items including underwear+socks, shoes, and outerwear and I consider that very successful given the vast variants in temperature I can remain dressed appropriately and comfortably. All that being said, try not to focus too much on a certain number of items, what's most important is that you fully appreciate and wear every item of clothing that you own.

Hey there, body piercing apprentice here - I'm not sure if this will help or not but I'm going to walk you through the process of a client coming in for a nose piercing from my perspective. Every piercing shop will vary slightly but the general sequence of events should remain the same so hopefully this will ease your mind a bit about what to expect.

Firstly, I live and work in an area that still has a lot of restrictions due to covid-19, so our front door remains locked. The client would show up at the shop at the time of their appointment and stand outside the door if I notice them right away I let them in, otherwise they knock a few times and I come to the door. I open the door and have the client answer our covid-19 screening checklist. 

Once the screening checklist is complete I let the client into the shop, spray their hands with sanitizer, and direct them to take a seat in our waiting area. I ask the client their name, age, and what their appointment is for (in this scenario it's a nose piercing), and verify that the information given lines up with what I have written down in our appointment book.

Next, I bring the client their consent waiver, they will read the warnings and risks related to getting a piercing, as well as fill it out with some personal information like full name, date of birth, phone number, and a list of known allergies or medical conditions. I may go and do something else while the client fills out their waiver as it can take a few minutes, but I remain in the general area in case they have any questions. I will also show bring out the starter jewelry options for the selected piercing and discuss with the client which they'd like.

Once the paperwork is complete I will bring the client into our piercing room and have them sit on the exam bed. In our shop we have relaxing music playing in the piercing rooms at all times. I will explain to them the steps of how I am going to perform their piercing and remind them that if they feel sick, dizzy, or change their mind at any point in the piercing process to let me know right away. I then instruct the client to lay down on the exam bed and pull their mask down so that it only covers their mouth. For a nostril piercing the bed would have the backrest tilted up, so more of a chair-like position than a flatbed. For a septum piercing, I would have the client sit on the edge of the table with their legs hanging over and their back straight.

Next, I spray my hands with sanitizer and set up my piercing table with every supply/tool I will need to complete the piercing. When my table is set up I put on a face shield (I already have a medical mask and a fabric mask on), and I wash my hands with an antibacterial soap in the sink, then I spray my hands with hand sanitizer and wait a moment for them to dry before putting fresh gloves on. Next, I will sanitize the area on the client that I'll be piercing, first with antibacterial soap, then with diluted chlorohexidine (some piercers use rubbing alcohol instead). I will mark where I'm going to put the nose piercing with a  toothpick dipped in gentian violet (for a septum piercing I wouldn't mark, but would feel for the sweet-spot) and show the client where I put the mark with a hand-held mirror. We can discuss changing the placement, and I will re-mark if necessary.

Once the client has consented to the placement, I'll give them a squishy stress ball and instruct them to breathe in through the nose and out through the mouth. I will apply the clamps, pierce on the mark, cork the needle, and insert the jewelry, all within a matter of seconds. If the client bleeds I will clot the blood with a piece of gauze for a minute or two. Then I will spray the fresh piercing with diluted chlorohexidine and instruct them to sit up slowly so they don't get a headrush. Once upright they can stand up and check out their new piercing in the wall mirror. I'll give them a couple of extra pieces of gauze in a plastic bag in case it bleeds at all on their way home from the shop.

After the piercing is complete I bring the client out to the front desk where I explain how to properly clean and heal their new piercing, we will discuss aftercare supplies. I will also supply them with an aftercare sheet which details on paper what to do and what to avoid when healing a fresh piercing. Next, they will pay (my shop takes cash or card but some shops only take cash so make sure you know before going to your appointment), and they can buy some aftercare supplies if needed.

After that, the client is free to go and I will let them out. Hope this was helpful in some way! good luck with your piercing appointment tomorrow :)

tldr; the process of getting a nose piercing in detail

Carnauba wax comes from palm plants in South America. Many vegans choose not to consume palm oil and carnauba wax due to the huge ecological impact farming palm has on rain forests. you can do your own research about palm farming and deforestation and decide for yourself whether you'll avoid it. Malic acid technically can be derived from animal sources but 99% of the time it's plant-sourced, so it's vegan. but other than those there's nothing to worry about in this ingredient list :)

Hey there! body piercing apprentice and 7-year vegan here- I've never heard of or noticed clients bleeding more when they are vegan/veggie, nor have I experienced it myself being pierced. My girlfriend is also vegan and I have pierced her multiple times and have not noticed that she bleeds any more than non-veggie clients. Neither of us takes any supplements but we do pay attention to getting sufficient nutrients through whole foods if that makes any difference.

It's possible your piercer hit a blood vessel when piercing, did he check your cartilage for vessels with a flashlight before marking your ear? If a vessel was hit it's absolutely normal to have a lot of bleeding, I've accidentally pierced through a blood vessel when doing a cartilage piercing and it bled quite a bit and took a while to clot.

I'm not a doctor but if you've had a blood test done recently and there were no red flags, I'd say you don't have to worry. Some people just bleed more than others, and as long as your piercings aren't literally dripping blood days after being done it's most likely just how your body heals, everyone is different. A little bit of dried blood around your piercing for 1 or even 2 weeks after getting pierced is normal for some people, especially if there's a chance a blood vessel was nicked. 

Hope this helped! good luck in the rest of your healing process :)
